newsitem.title: USA: Bridgestone unit says sees record FY96.
newsitem.headline: Bridgestone unit says sees record FY96.

text.p: Bridgestone Corp's U.S. unit, Bridgestone/Firestone Inc, said Wednesday it expects to have record sales and income this year despite a bitter, two-year strike by the United Steelworkers of America (USWA) union.
The Nashville-based unit and the union reached a tentative pact Tuesday, which must still be ratified by union members.

"We are expected to have record sales this year and record income for Bridgestone/Firestone," spokesman Trevor Hoskins said in a telephone interview. "Our sales have increased (and) our market share has increased in the last two years."
Bridgestone/Firestone has said previously that it forecast $6 billion in sales and $180 million in income for 1996 "and we are on target for that," Hoskins said.
The union's boycott and "corporate campaign" against the company did not work, he said.
The new agreement covers more than 6,000 workers at four tire plants and three other facilities, some of which were not involved in the strike, Hoskins said.
Plants operated throughout the strike, which began in July 1994.
Asked whether the pact would mean increased production and rubber demand, Hoskins said both have been "way above normal" throughout most of the strike.

"Because we went to seven-day operations in these plants, which were previously at five days, at the end of 1994, we have been producing many more tires than we did before this dispute started," Hoskins said.
The U.S. unit will make 41 million tires in 1996, nearly double the 21 million it made five years ago, he said.
He said the company is selling all the tires it can produce and has no inventory in stock.
Bridgestone/Firestone said in a statement it is "very satisfied" with the tentative agreement and is optimistic it will be ratified by union members.
As reported earlier Wednesday, union president George Becker has said some issues remain to be worked out.

But Bridgestone/Firestone chairman and chief executive officer Masatoshi Ono said in the statement, "We now look forward to establishing a partnership with the USWA and continuing to grow our business."
Masatoshi said despite the strike, the unit increased production and sales, raised productivity and cut costs.
About the agreement, he said, "We achieved all of (our) goals and we conceded in areas where we believed it was necessary to obtain a mutually satisfactory agreement."
About 4,000 members of the former United Rubber Workers union (now part of USWA) walked off the job at three U.S. tire plants and two other facilities in July 1994.

The union began a boycott of Bridgestone and Firestone brand products last year after the company said it had hired 2,000 replacement workers. Later the union offered an unconditional return to work. The company said most workers have been recalled, leaving fewer than 100 out of work.
